t: Maximum Number of Removal Queries That Can Be Processed I — Interval Expansion DP
o: Processing queries consumes elements from the two ends of nums, like a deque game. The one-time 'replace with a subsequence' operation is optimally used to delete a prefix and suffix upfront (middle elements are unreachable anyway), so the state space is simply (front removals f, back removals b). Let dp[f][b] = maximum number of queries processed having consumed f front and b back elements. From a state, if the next query fits nums[f] we may advance f, or if it fits nums[n-1-b] we may advance b. Processing states in order of f+b makes this a clean DAG relaxation. Example 3 shows why truncation matters: from the truncated [4,3] we process 2 queries.
k: Deleting middle elements never helps, so the free operation is exactly 'choose initial f and b'.
dp[f][b] relaxed in increasing f+b order yields the optimum in O(n^2); the answer is the maximum dp value.

a.n: Approach 1: O(n^2) DP over (front, back) removals
a.i: Initialize dp[f][b] = 0 for all f+b ≤ n (free truncation at the start). Sweep s = f+b ascending; for each state with value t < q, if nums[f] ≥ queries[t] relax dp[f+1][b] with t+1, and if nums[n-1-b] ≥ queries[t] relax dp[f][b+1] with t+1. Track the global maximum.
s: Allocate dp of size (n+1)×(n+1), all zeros.
For s = 0..n-1, for f = 0..s with b = s-f: attempt both end-removal transitions.
Return the maximum dp value seen (including fully consumed states).
a.t: O(n^2) — one relaxation per (f, b) state with f+b ≤ n; n ≤ 1000 gives ~5·10^5 states

w: Key justification for interviews: the subsequence operation only matters at the start, and only trimming the ends affects future choices, hence initializing all states to 0 models it exactly. Pitfalls: guarding f < n-b and b < n-f (cannot remove past the other end), and capturing answers at states where processing stopped early. Follow-up: the Hard version with n up to 2·10^5 needs a divide-and-conquer or greedy refinement of this DP.
